title: India's Crude Imports Rise In September As Oil Bill Surges Sharply
excerpt: Volumes hit a 2026 high as Gulf supply returned through Hormuz, but war-driven prices, freight and insurance kept the import bill climbing far faster.
body:
• India's crude imports rose about 7% in September while the import bill surged roughly 47%, according to The Hindu's report of official data — price, not volume, did most of the damage.
  • Tanker tracking put September arrivals at a 2026 high of about 5.26 million barrels a day, with Gulf supplies rebounding about 74% as Hormuz traffic partly recovered.
  • Iraq became the second-largest supplier again; Russian volumes slipped to about 1.74 million barrels a day, their lowest since April.
  • Track the official monthly figures yourself at the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), the oil ministry's data arm.

India bought more crude oil in September — and paid vastly more for it. Crude imports rose about 7% in the month while the import bill surged roughly 47%, The Hindu reported on Friday, a combination that captures India's energy problem in one line: volumes are recovering as Gulf supply returns, but every barrel now arrives at war-driven prices, with freight and insurance costs layered on top. The underlying monthly data are published by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), the oil ministry's statistics arm.

Tanker-tracking estimates tell the same story from the shipping side. Kpler data put India's September arrivals at about 5.26 million barrels per day, the highest monthly level of 2026 and roughly 600,000 barrels a day above August, according to an analysis of the September flows. Supplies from West Asia rose about 74% in a month to roughly 2.1 million barrels a day, lifting the region's share to 39.5% from 26% in August — close to the pre-conflict mix.

The bill was already climbing

September extended a pattern set over the summer. India's crude import bill for April-August reached $74.8 billion, up 48.4% on a year earlier, even though volumes over those five months slipped 0.4% to 100.7 million tonnes, PPAC data cited by OilPrice.com showed. In other words, India paid about $24.4 billion more for slightly less oil. Freight on the Ras Tanura-to-India route had risen more than 400% since late February, when the conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz to normal traffic, and the Indian crude basket averaged $114.80 a barrel in early September.

Gulf barrels return, Russian share slips

The supplier table rotated in September. Russia remained the largest single source at about 1.74 million barrels a day, but that was its lowest since April, down from 2.02 million in August. Iraq moved back into second place at about 525,000 barrels a day — more than three times its August level — followed by Saudi Arabia at about 517,000. Signal Group data cited by India Seatrade News put Iraqi shipments at 4.41 million tonnes in September, up 106.3% on August, after a near-cessation between March and July.

The mechanics of the trade have changed too. Indian refiners including Indian Oil, Reliance Industries, Bharat Petroleum and HPCL-Mittal Energy are increasingly buying Iraqi crude on a free-on-board basis and chartering tankers themselves — taking freight-rate and voyage risk onto their own books rather than paying sellers a delivered premium. With VLCC earnings on Gulf routes among the highest in the market and war-risk premiums for Hormuz transits quoted at 6% to 9% of vessel value, that shift makes shipping a first-order cost in procurement, not an afterthought.

What it means for the economy

At more than 5 million barrels a day and prices above $100, India's crude bill runs at well over $500 million a day, so sustained high prices widen the trade deficit, pressure the rupee and complicate the Reserve Bank's inflation task through fuel, freight and fertiliser costs. Gulf grades at least help operationally: Middle East crude yields more diesel, the tightest part of the global fuel market, which suits India's demand slate. The risk is concentration — Gulf and Russian barrels together supply roughly three-quarters of India's crude, so a renewed shock to either flow cannot be replaced quickly. October tanker loadings and the commerce ministry's detailed trade release will show whether September's Gulf recovery holds.
